title: One Guru, many voices
hookLine: Sikhs honor the Bhagats' hymns as fully part of the Guru

cards: Someone walks into the gurdwara hall, takes off their shoes, covers their head, and walks up the aisle toward the Granth under its canopy. They kneel and touch their forehead to the floor.
A small question hides in that bow: which part of the book is it for? The Gurus' hymns? The pages of Kabir, the pages of Farid, the minstrels' Var?
Nobody bows to a chapter. The bow goes to the whole Granth at once.

teach.h: THE GRANTH IS THE GURU, PRESENT.
teach.b: Sikhs call the Granth the Guru Granth Sahib, and they mean Guru: not a book about the Guru, but the Guru present, honored as a living teacher.
Sikhs say Guru Gobind Singh passed the guruship to the Granth, and since then there has been no human Guru. Now count the voices in it.
The Gurus wrote under one name: their hymns carry the signature Nanak, whether the hymn is by Guru Nanak or Guru Arjan or another Guru, and a heading marked Mahala tells you which.
Many hands, one name. Then the Bhagats, from different trades and towns and paths, with their own names in the headings. Then the Bhatts' swayyas, the minstrels' Var, Sundar's Sadd.
Different voices from different times and places, some from Hindu backgrounds, some Muslim. Sikhs don't treat these as layers of lesser and greater.
Guru Ram Das, in Raag Nat on Ang 982, says in paraphrase that the bani is the Guru and the Guru is the bani. The word itself is the teacher. That line is the key to this whole block.
If the word is the Guru, then every word in the Guru's book is the Guru's word, whoever's mouth it first came from.
Kabir's line and Guru Nanak's get the same canopy, the same chauri waved over them, the same morning opening and evening rest. Not one voice: one Guru speaking through many voices.

how: Sikhs bow before the Guru Granth Sahib as the living Guru, opening it each morning and laying it to rest each evening, and every hymn in it, the Gurus' and the Bhagats', is honored in the same way.

games.q: you're bowing before the Guru Granth Sahib. a friend asks which part of the book the bow is for. what do you say?
o: the whole Granth, every voice in it.
whichever page happens to be open.
games.why: Sikhs honor the whole Granth as the Guru, so one bow covers the Gurus, the Bhagats and the minstrels alike.

practice: Picture the whole book closed under its cloth, every voice inside it: the Gurus, the Bhagats, the minstrels.

If you're near a gurdwara or a Granth today, you can let one bow carry all of it in mind; for now, breathe with the picture, with Waheguru on each breath out if you pray, and lower your head slightly at the end, a small bow.
